interactions.label: Why must immediate stabilisation (oxygen, positioning, airway support) precede t

params.question: Why must immediate stabilisation (oxygen, positioning, airway support) precede treatment of the underlying cause in a child with respiratory distress?

answers.text: Respiratory failure and arrest can follow decompensation within minutes, so securing the airway and oxygenation takes priority

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. The spectrum from compensated distress to arrest can progress in minutes. All immediate management — oxygen, positioning, airway support — must precede aetiological investigation.

answers.text: Clinical signs are unreliable during active distress, so the aetiology cannot be determined until the child is stabilised

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Clinical signs can be assessed during distress. The real priority is that respiratory failure and arrest can follow within minutes once compensation is lost — there may not be time to treat the cause if the child arrests.

answers.text: Aetiological treatments such as antibiotics and bronchodilators are contraindicated during active respiratory distress

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: These treatments are not contraindicated during distress. The reason for stabilising first is that a child progressing beyond compensation can arrest within minutes — no cause-specific treatment will help an arrested child.

answers.text: Respiratory distress in children is usually self-limiting and resolves with supportive care alone

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Respiratory distress in children is NOT usually self-limiting. Without intervention, compensated distress can progress rapidly through decompensation and failure to arrest.

overallFeedback.feedback: The key principle is that respiratory failure and arrest can follow decompensation within minutes. Stabilisation (oxygen, positioning, airway support) must come first because no cause-specific treatment will work if the child arrests.

Exactly right. Stabilisation is time-critical because the progression from compensated distress to respiratory arrest can be rapid — the underlying cause matters, but only a stable child can be investigated and treated.

interactions.label: Why was the earlier 30-minute definition of status epilepticus replaced by the c

params.question: Why was the earlier 30-minute definition of status epilepticus replaced by the current 5-minute operational threshold (t1)?

answers.text: Because 30 minutes was too short — most seizures that last 30 minutes still stop spontaneously

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The 30-minute threshold was too LONG, not too short. Seizures lasting beyond 5 minutes almost never stop spontaneously, and waiting 30 minutes meant treating far too late.

answers.text: Because seizures lasting >5 minutes almost never stop spontaneously, and benzodiazepine efficacy declines with every minute of delay

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Two converging pieces of evidence drove the change: seizures lasting >5 minutes rarely self-terminate, and benzodiazepines become progressively less effective with each passing minute of untreated seizure.

answers.text: Because MRI studies demonstrated that irreversible brain damage begins at exactly 5 minutes

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The 5-minute threshold is not based on MRI evidence of damage starting at 5 minutes. Long-term neurological consequences are associated with t2 (>30 minutes). The t1 threshold reflects the operational point where the seizure is unlikely to self-terminate.

answers.text: Because the 30-minute definition required continuous EEG monitoring that is unavailable in most emergency settings

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The 30-minute definition was a clinical one, not dependent on EEG. It was replaced because waiting 30 minutes allowed unnecessary neuronal injury and critically reduced the effectiveness of benzodiazepine treatment.

overallFeedback.feedback: The 30-minute threshold was replaced because seizures lasting >5 minutes almost never stop spontaneously, and benzodiazepine efficacy declines progressively with each passing minute. The current operational threshold (t1 = ≥5 minutes) ensures earlier treatment.

Well done. The shift from 30 to 5 minutes reflects two key insights: seizures persisting beyond 5 minutes almost never self-terminate, and benzodiazepines work best when given early — each minute of delay reduces their efficacy.

interactions.label: A child in hypovolaemic shock with cold extremities has an SpO₂ reading of 98%.

params.question: A child in hypovolaemic shock with cold extremities has an SpO₂ reading of 98%. Which interpretation is most appropriate?

answers.text: The child has adequate oxygenation and does not need supplemental oxygen

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: An SpO₂ of 98% in a poorly perfused child cannot be trusted at face value. Pulse oximetry depends on adequate pulsatile blood flow — in shock with vasoconstriction, readings may not reflect true arterial saturation.

answers.text: The reading is accurate but incomplete — the child also needs capnography because SpO₂ does not measure CO₂

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: While it is true that SpO₂ does not detect hypercapnia, the primary concern here is the reliability of the reading itself. In hypovolaemic shock with cold extremities, the pulsatile signal is diminished, making the SpO₂ value unreliable.

answers.text: The reading is likely unreliable because pulse oximetry requires adequate peripheral perfusion to generate accurate values

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. SpO₂ readings are unreliable when the perfusion waveform is poor. Shock, hypothermia, and severe peripheral vasoconstriction all reduce the pulsatile signal the oximeter depends on — clinical assessment must supplement the number.

answers.text: The SpO₂ confirms that respiratory support can be safely discontinued and focus shifted to fluid resuscitation alone

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Never discontinue respiratory support based solely on an SpO₂ reading in a poorly perfused child. The value may be falsely reassuring — pulse oximetry requires adequate pulsatile blood flow, which is compromised in hypovolaemic shock.

overallFeedback.feedback: In hypovolaemic shock with cold extremities, the SpO₂ reading is unreliable. Pulse oximetry depends on pulsatile blood flow — when perfusion is poor (shock, hypothermia, vasoconstriction), readings may not reflect true arterial saturation. Never rely on the number alone.

Excellent analysis. In hypovolaemic shock with peripheral vasoconstriction, pulse oximetry readings are unreliable because the device depends on adequate pulsatile blood flow. Always correlate SpO₂ with clinical signs.
